justification:
All four round-1 citation errors are now correct, verified independently against the fetched RFC 8446 plaintext by line number rather than by re-trusting the writer's claim. (1) 'The certificate of the endpoint and any per-certificate extensions' (Certificate message definition) is now cited to section 2 and does live there (absolute lines 684-693, inside section 2's span 511-1036) — the numbered subsection 4.4.2 (3535-3653) defines the wire format instead, in different wording. (2) 'A signature over the entire handshake using the private key corresponding to the public key in the Certificate message' (CertificateVerify definition) is now cited to section 2 and does live there (lines 686-694), not in 4.4.3 (3823-3944). (3) Finished's 'provides key confirmation, binds the endpoint's identity to the exchanged keys, and in PSK mode also authenticates the handshake' is now cited to section 2 and does live there (lines 699-702), not 4.4.4. (4) 'All handshake messages after the ServerHello are now encrypted' is now cited explicitly to section 1.2 and is verbatim there (absolute line 428, inside 1.2's span 405-510) rather than left as an ambiguous 'same section' pointing at section 2, where it does not appear. Note that section 4.4.4 is still correctly cited elsewhere in the same paragraph for the `verify_data = HMAC(finished_key, Transcript-Hash(...))` formula, which genuinely is defined there (confirmed at line ~3998, inside 4.4.4) — the fix was surgical, not a blanket find-replace of every 4.4.x citation, exactly as round 1's fixLooksLike guidance asked for.

The toolchain statement is present and correctly placed: 'Code on this page was run with the .NET 10 SDK (10.0.401) on Windows 11, x64:' appears in the writer's own words, immediately before the article's first executed code block (the AEAD demo), not as a stamped opening sentence — this matches both the round-1 finding's fixLooksLike and the editorial brief's 'not as a stamped opening sentence' rule. The two unsourced claims are now properly scoped to what RFC 8446 section 1 actually supports: the padding sentence now reads 'Padding is optional, and RFC 8446 does not say how many servers turn it on... enough, in principle, to distinguish one page on a site from another when their sizes differ' — this drops the unsupported 'most servers do not use it' adoption-rate assertion and the unqualified fingerprinting-difficulty claim, replacing both with language the RFC's own sentence ('TLS does not hide the length of the data it transmits, though endpoints are able to pad TLS records...to obscure lengths and improve protection against traffic analysis techniques', verified verbatim at RFC 8446 section 1) actually supports. The one addition not requested by round 1 — 'or when' (timing) in the topic sentence — is an observation about network-level packet visibility so basic it needs no citation (any observer on the path sees packet timestamps by definition of watching the wire); it is not a new unsupported empirical claim in the same class as the ones that were softened.

The round-2 diff also adds two new inline citations not required by round 1 (AesGcm Class's 'represents an Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) key to be used with the Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) mode of operation', and HMACSHA256.HashData's 'computes the HMAC of data using the SHA-256 algorithm'), both already present in front matter's source list from round 1 and both verified verbatim on the live Microsoft Learn pages today. These strictly improve the article — the primitives that get runnable demos now also get their own one-line MS Learn citation, matching the pattern already used for AesGcm.Decrypt, ECDiffieHellman.DeriveKeyFromHash and ECDsa.SignHash.

Code verification: all 7 executable blocks pass `tools/run-code.mjs` on 4 consecutive runs today, including the live network-dependent example.com chain walk and the local self-signed-server exercise; zero flakiness. I also re-read the whole article fresh rather than diffing only the flagged passages, checking exercise placement (no predict-the-output exercise shows its output before the solution — confirmed for all three exercises), heading variety (no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion), the RFC 5280 chain-of-trust quotes (still verbatim and correctly placed in section 3.2, unchanged from round 1 and reconfirmed by line offset), and the cross-links (both linked sibling articles, how-the-internet-works.md and http-explained.md, exist in this worktree's content tree, so no crosslinks file is required).

What keeps this at 9.0 rather than higher: one round-1 minor finding is still open and untouched by the fix commit — the article's only live certificate-error exercise demonstrates an untrusted root (RemoteCertificateChainErrors) and never mentions, attempts, or acknowledges the absence of a name-mismatch (RemoteCertificateNameMismatch) demonstration, which is arguably the padlock failure a reader is more likely to have actually seen in a browser. Round 1 explicitly scored this as minor and not requiring a live network call to fix (a second local self-signed server with a mismatched SAN would suffice), and it remains true today that this is a coverage gap rather than an error — nothing in the article is wrong, it just doesn't cover this one adjacent failure mode. That is a nit at MDN/Real Python quality, not a blocker, so it does not cap the score the way a factual error would, but it is real and unaddressed.
